title: Actively open-minded thinking
summary: A thinking disposition, named by Jonathan Baron, in which a person searches thoroughly and fairly for possibilities, evidence and goals, gives weight to evidence against a favoured view, and holds confidence in proportion to the search actually done.

title: Affirming the consequent
summary: The deductively invalid inference that takes a conditional "if P then Q" together with the truth of Q and concludes P, treating a sufficient condition as if it were also a necessary one.
criticalQuestions: Besides the stated antecedent, what else could make the consequent true?
Does the conditional really run both ways, or has a one-way "if" been heard as "if and only if"?
How often does the consequent occur when the antecedent is false, and has that rate been checked?
Have rival explanations of the observed consequent been compared before accepting the antecedent?

title: Alfred Tarski
summary: Polish-American logician and mathematician (1901-1983) whose 1933 definition of truth for formal languages and 1936 model-theoretic definition of logical consequence gave modern logic its standard account of what it means for an argument to be valid.

title: Amos Tversky
summary: Israeli-American cognitive psychologist (1937-1996) who, largely with Daniel Kahneman, showed that intuitive judgment under uncertainty relies on a few heuristics that produce systematic biases, and who co-created prospect theory.

title: Anchoring effect
summary: The tendency for a numerical estimate or judgment to be pulled toward a previously encountered value (the anchor), even when that value is uninformative or plainly arbitrary.

title: Argument
summary: A set of statements in which one or more premises are offered as reasons in support of a further statement, the conclusion; the basic unit that logic and critical thinking evaluate.

title: Aristotle
summary: Greek philosopher (384-322 BCE), student of Plato and founder of the Lyceum, who created the first systematic formal logic, the syllogistic, and wrote the first classification of fallacies; his logical treatises, later collected as the Organon, set the agenda for logic for two thousand years.

title: Base-rate neglect
summary: The error of judging how likely something is from case-specific evidence alone while ignoring or underweighting how common it is in the first place (its base rate or prior probability).
criticalQuestions: Before looking at this evidence, how common is the outcome in the relevant population?
How often would this same evidence show up if the outcome were absent (the false-positive rate)?
Out of 1,000 comparable cases, how many would show the evidence and actually have the outcome?
Is the base rate I am using drawn from a reference class that really fits this case?

title: Bias blind spot
summary: The tendency to see cognitive and motivational biases more readily in other people's judgments than in one's own, so that people rate themselves as less biased than their peers.

title: Chrysippus
summary: Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 280-207 BCE) and third head of the Stoa, the main architect of Stoic logic, whose system of five indemonstrable arguments, starting with "if p then q; p; therefore q", made him one of the first to organise propositional logic as a discipline.

title: Consider the opposite
summary: A debiasing technique in which a person deliberately generates reasons why their current judgment, hypothesis or reference value might be wrong, so that evidence pointing the other way becomes as available as the evidence that supports it.

title: Daniel Kahneman
summary: Israeli-American psychologist (1934-2024) who co-founded the heuristics-and-biases program with Amos Tversky, won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics, and popularized the fast/slow (System 1 / System 2) account of intuition and deliberation.

title: Deductive reasoning
summary: Reasoning in which the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion, so that if the argument is valid it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.

title: Falsifiability criterion
summary: Karl Popper's proposal that a claim or theory counts as scientific only if some possible observation could show it to be false; a theory that is compatible with every conceivable outcome tells us nothing testable about the world.

title: Gettier problem
aliases: problem of epistemic luck in the analysis of knowledge
summary: The problem, raised by Edmund Gettier in 1963, that a person can hold a justified, true belief that still falls short of knowledge because it is true only by luck; it shows that justified true belief is not sufficient for knowing.

title: Heuristics and biases program
summary: The research program, launched by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman around 1970, that explains intuitive judgment under uncertainty as the use of a few general-purpose heuristics (such as representativeness, availability and anchoring) which are usually serviceable but produce predictable, systematic errors when compared with normative rules.

title: Informal logic
summary: The branch of logic that develops non-formal standards and procedures for identifying, interpreting, evaluating and constructing the arguments people actually make in natural language, in settings such as public debate, law, medicine, education and the workplace.

title: Judgment and decision making
summary: The interdisciplinary research field, rooted in psychology, that studies how people form judgments (estimates, predictions, probabilities) and make choices, typically by comparing actual behavior with normative standards such as probability theory and expected utility and then designing ways to close the gap.

title: Lateral reading
summary: A source-evaluation technique, borrowed from professional fact checkers, in which you leave an unfamiliar website early and search other sources about who is behind it before judging its content, instead of scrutinising the page itself.

title: Method of counterexample
summary: A test for invalidity: to show that an argument form does not guarantee its conclusion, describe a case or substitution instance of the same form in which every premise is true and the conclusion is false.

title: Modus ponens
summary: The valid inference form "if P then Q; P; therefore Q", which concludes the consequent of a conditional from the conditional together with its antecedent.

title: Natural frequency format
summary: A way of presenting or re-expressing risk information as counts of cases drawn from one concrete reference group (for example "8 of the 10 people with the condition test positive") instead of as conditional probabilities, so that the base rate stays visible and Bayesian updating becomes simple counting.

title: Organon
summary: The collection of Aristotle's six logical treatises (Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics and On Sophistical Refutations), assembled and named "tool" by later Peripatetic commentators, which served as the standard textbook of logic in the Arabic and Latin traditions for some two thousand years.

title: Posterior Analytics
summary: Aristotle's two-book treatise (4th century BCE) on demonstration and scientific knowledge, which argues that a proof yields knowledge only when its premises are true, primary and explanatory, and that the chain of proof must end in first principles grasped without demonstration.

title: Premortem
summary: A plan-evaluation technique in which a team, before committing to a plan, imagines that it has already been carried out and has failed, then has each member independently write down the reasons it failed so those risks can be addressed in advance.

title: Principle of charity
summary: The interpretive norm that, before criticising what someone has argued, you should reconstruct their claims and reasoning in the most reasonable form the text and context plausibly allow, rather than in a weaker or distorted form.

title: Soundness
summary: The property of a deductive argument that is valid and whose premises are all actually true; a sound argument therefore guarantees a true conclusion.

title: Stephen Toulmin
summary: British-born philosopher (1922-2009) whose book The Uses of Argument (1958) challenged the idea that good reasoning must take the form of formal deduction and gave argumentation theory its claim-data-warrant layout.

title: Straw man fallacy
summary: The fallacy of replacing an opponent's actual position with a distorted, weaker or invented version, refuting that substitute, and presenting the refutation as if it defeated the real position.
criticalQuestions: Would the other side recognise this description as their own position, stated in their own terms?
Is the view being refuted what was actually said, or an exaggerated, absolute or invented version of it?
If the weakest argument has been answered, have the stronger arguments for the same conclusion been addressed too?
Who exactly holds the position being attacked, or is it attributed only to a vague "some people"?
Does refuting this version leave the original claim standing?

title: Toulmin model of argument
summary: Stephen Toulmin's six-part layout for analysing practical arguments: a claim supported by data, licensed by a warrant that rests on backing, tempered by a qualifier and open to rebuttal.

title: Validity
summary: The property of a deductive argument whose form makes it impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false; validity concerns the link between premises and conclusion, not whether the premises are actually true.
